harnessExplanation.role: The Laws tab (Tests.lawspec) says what must be true. Solution implements the function. Harness.lawspec describes how to choose inputs for the generated property checks.
harnessExplanation.declaration: The first line names this harness, then for names the unit from Tests.lawspec that it tests. A strategy is a recipe for drawing values. :: introduces its type; where restricts its values; any asks the testing engine to generate values of that type. for law selects a named property, and use binds a strategy to one of its quantified inputs.
harnessExplanation.scope: A strategy changes the inputs sampled, not the requirement in Laws. A passing sample says only that the checks passed for the inputs tried. It is not a proof, and changing a generator to avoid a failure does not repair a bug or a false claim.
harnessExplanation.execution: The generated test runner is also called a harness. You edit the LawSpec configuration here; the compiler builds the runner that calls your implementation and records results. Run checks executes the set shown beneath the button: Examples + boundaries selects concrete and boundary checks; Sampled properties selects generated property cases; All checks includes both. Each step selects its teaching mode; Test controls also offers explicitly named alternate runs. Seed repeats generation under the same code, generator and tool versions; Replay failure also uses the recorded path to the failing case. F# runs through Fable and the JavaScript runner with fast-check in this browser, separately from native .NET/FsCheck.

stages.title: The calculator knows one answer
story: We want a calculator that adds two integers. By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain why a passing test can leave a wrong calculator undetected, and strengthen its checks.
Our first promise is just 1 + 2 = 3. In Solution, add recognizes that pair and returns 3. Every other pair returns 0. Predict what happens on 2 and 2, but keep the test unchanged for this first run.

There are three tabs: Laws states the promises, Solution contains the function, and Harness configures generated test inputs. For now the harness has no strategy: the concrete test already supplies 1 and 2. You can open Harness at any point and expand its explanation below the editor.
Run the example. It checks the one promise we wrote. Ask what evidence we have for the other branch of the function.
stages.action: Run the example. Explain why the function can pass it while still returning 0 on 2 and 2.
stages.reason: One successful call establishes one observed answer. Our goal is a function that also handles unfamiliar inputs.
stages.expect: The supplied code compiles and the selected checks pass. Read which checks actually ran before interpreting this result.
stages.recovery: Reset this step restores its supplied files and seed. After an edit, use the actual result to judge your version; the story’s prediction describes the supplied files.
stages.syntax: In Laws, add :: Int32 -> Int32 -> Int32 declares two integer inputs and an integer result. add 1 2 calls the function; = 3 compares its result with 3. law onePlusTwo names this claim, and definition contains the Boolean expression to check.

stages.title: Compare a call with its reversed call
story: For addition, swapping the two inputs should leave the answer unchanged. Laws names this relationship swapInputs: it compares add x y with add y x.

Where do x and y come from? Open Harness. A harness connects a law to a strategy: a recipe for test data. Here numbers chooses integers from -2 through 2. The two use lines feed separate draws into x and y of swapInputs. Laws supplies the comparison; the harness supplies its inputs.
Our calculator remembers 1 + 2 but not 2 + 1. Use Run checks with All checks and inspect the sampled failure. A relationship has exposed an answer we never listed as a concrete test.
stages.action: Use Run checks with All checks. Use the reported inputs to trace both calls to add, and explain why their results differ.
stages.reason: This property can reject an implementation that memorizes particular input orders.
stages.expect: The supplied code compiles, then the selected checks fail. A compiler error is a different problem; inspect diagnostics if execution did not start.
stages.recovery: Reset this step restores its supplied files and seed. After an edit, use the actual result to judge your version; the story’s prediction describes the supplied files.
stages.syntax: for all introduces the quantified inputs x and y. In Harness, :: introduces the strategy’s type, where bounds its values and any requests generation. for law swapInputs selects the claim; use supplies its inputs. The claim allows -10 through 10, but this recipe samples only -2 through 2.
harnessNotes: numbers draws Int32 integers from -2 through 2, including both endpoints. The variable n describes each candidate value inside the strategy; it is not a separate input to add.

for law swapInputs selects the claim in Laws. use numbers for x and use numbers for y draw the two inputs separately from that recipe. The law permits -10 through 10; this strategy samples a smaller region, so a passing sample cannot establish the whole claim.

module Solution

let sort (xs: int list) : int list = []
fsharp.Tests.lawspec:
-- ref:DEC-learn-tests-in-lawspec
unit learn.sorting
sort :: List Int32 -> List Int32

function ordered (xs :: List Int32) -> Bool is
  first matching case of xs :
    when Nil then true
    when Cons h t then
      (first matching case of t :
        when Nil then true
        when Cons next rest then h <= next and ordered t
      end case)
  end case
end function

law emptyInput is
  definition:
    sort [] = []
  end definition
end law

law sortingRule is
  definition:
    for all (xs :: List Int32) => ordered (sort xs) = true end for all
  end definition
end law

end unit

  end strategy

  end for law
